videos.script: Somebody tells you their internet is slow. What do they mean? {{question}} Almost always they mean one of three completely different things, and the three have different causes, different fixes, and almost nothing to do with each other. {{three}} The first is how much fits through at once. That is bandwidth, and it is what you are sold. The second is how long one thing takes to get there and back. That is latency, and nobody sells it to you at all. The third is what you actually end up with, which is usually neither of the first two. That is throughput. {{names}} Here is why this matters. Pay twice as much and double your bandwidth, and a page that was slow will very often be exactly as slow — because for a small transfer, bandwidth was never what was holding it up. {{doubling}} By the end of this lesson you will be able to listen to somebody describe a problem, and say which of the three they are actually describing. Which, when you are the person being asked to fix it, is most of the work. {{title}}

Three tools, and each one answers a different question. Watch what they actually say, and what they quietly do not. {{tools}} First, a speed test. It reports a big number and everybody stops reading there. But look at what it did to get that number: it opened many connections at once, to a server your provider chose, usually one very close to you. {{speedtest}} That is a measurement of the best case, on purpose. It is the right way to answer is my line delivering what I pay for, and it is the wrong way to answer why is this website slow — because that website is not next door and your browser is not opening sixteen connections to it. {{best-case}} Notice the latency number in the corner, the one nobody looks at. Now start a large download and run the test again. {{under-load}} Watch that number. On a lot of connections it goes from twenty milliseconds to three hundred, and that is the queue we spent a whole section on, appearing on a screen in front of you. The line is not broken. It is full, and the buffer is doing exactly what it was built to do. {{bufferbloat}} Second, ping. One small packet, there and back, timed. This is the cleanest number in networking, and it measures one thing only: the round trip to that host, right now. {{ping}} What it does not tell you is anything about capacity. A machine can answer a ping in eight milliseconds and still take a minute to send you a file. {{ping-limit}} Third, traceroute. A list of the machines in between, built the way we described in lesson two, one expired hop counter at a time. {{traceroute}} Read it carefully, because it lies in two specific ways. A blank line does not mean a broken hop; it means a router that declined to answer, which is entirely allowed. And a high number on hop six does not mean hop six is slow — those replies come from the router itself, which treats making them as the least important thing it does. {{traceroute-lies}} What traceroute is genuinely good for is the shape of the whole list. Where does the geography change. Where does the time jump and stay jumped. That step, the one that goes up and never comes back down, is the one worth asking about. {{shape}}
